label: Full Game Transition
title: Transitioning to the full game
lead: What changes when Casualties Unknown leaves the demo, what breaks in a mod compiled against it, and how to ship one DLL that runs on both.
bodyHtml:
Why the full game breaks demo-compiled mods

The demo is frozen. The full game keeps changing. A DLL you compiled against the demo's Assembly-CSharp carries hard references to the exact shape of every type and method it touches, and the CLR resolves those references when the game JITs your code. When the full game reshapes something you referenced, that resolution fails at runtime — often inside a Harmony-patched game method, which takes the whole patch family down with it.

There are two failure classes to plan for:

  • Method signature changes. A method gains, loses, or reorders parameters. A [HarmonyPatch] pinned to the old signature can no longer find its target and throws ArgumentException: Undefined target method during PatchAll().
  • Member-shape changes. A field becomes a property (or a member is renamed). Code compiled against the field emits ldfld/stfld; on the property build the JIT throws MissingFieldException: Field not found. This one is easy to miss because a signature-only diff between demo and full looks clean.

The goal is one DLL that runs on the demo, the Playtest build, and the full game without recompiling per build. Everything below is about reaching that.

Detecting which build is running

CUCoreLib exposes a single cached build-detection seam. CUCoreUtils.IsDemo() scans loaded assemblies for full-game-only types and requires two or more distinct matches before it declares the full game, so a mod that happens to add one same-named type won't fool it.

GameBuildInfo wraps that check, and [AppliesToBuild] lets a Harmony patch family declare which builds it targets. CUCoreLib applies patch families individually and skips a mismatched family before its targets resolve, so full-game-only patches never throw on the demo.

MemberMeaning
CUCoreUtils.IsDemo()true on the demo, false on the full game. Cached after the first call.
GameBuildInfo.CurrentThe running GameBuild (Demo or Full).
GameBuildInfo.IsFullGameShorthand for !IsDemo().
GameBuildInfo.Matches(GameBuild)true when the target flag includes the running build. GameBuild.Both matches everything.
[AppliesToBuild(GameBuild.Full)]Restricts a patch family to the full game. Families without it apply to every build.
 
using CUCoreLib.Helpers;

if (GameBuildInfo.IsFullGame)
{
    // Full-game-only behavior.
}

// Gate an entire Harmony family to one build:
[AppliesToBuild(GameBuild.Full)]
[HarmonyPatch(typeof(SomeFullGameOnlyType), "SomeMethod")]
public static class FullGameOnlyPatch
{
    // Skipped cleanly on the demo; never resolves its target there.
}

Known break: Body.Eat gained a foodType parameter

On the demo, Body.Eat is Eat(float hungerAmount, float weightGain). On the full game it is Eat(float hungerAmount, float weightGain, int foodType). A patch attribute pinned to Eat(float, float) stops resolving on the full game.

The fix has two parts. First, use a name-only Harmony target. [HarmonyPatch(typeof(Body), "Eat")] with no argument types binds at runtime to whichever single Eat overload exists, so the same attribute works on both builds. Second, when you need to call Eat yourself, go through reflection so the parameter list adapts to the loaded build.

using System.Reflection;
using HarmonyLib;

internal static class BodyEat
{
    private static readonly MethodInfo EatMethod = AccessTools.Method(typeof(Body), "Eat");
    private static readonly bool HasFoodType =
        EatMethod != null && EatMethod.GetParameters().Length >= 3;

    // foodType: 0 = neutral, 1 = the "half hunger, adds sickness" type, 2 = vomit-and-refuse.
    internal static void Invoke(Body body, float hungerAmount, float weightGain, int foodType)
    {
        if (body == null || EatMethod == null) return;
        var args = HasFoodType
            ? new object[] { hungerAmount, weightGain, foodType }
            : new object[] { hungerAmount, weightGain };
        EatMethod.Invoke(body, args);
    }
}

// Name-only target: resolves on demo AND full.
[HarmonyPatch(typeof(Body), "Eat")]
public static class InfiniteSteakPatch
{
    [HarmonyPostfix]
    private static void Postfix(Body __instance)
    {
        BodyEat.Invoke(__instance, 15f, 1.6f, 1);
    }
}

MethodInfo.Invoke on a Harmony-patched method still runs your prefix/postfix chain, so ordering contracts are preserved. On the full game foodType is meaningful: charType == 1 && foodType == 1 halves hunger and adds sickness; charType == 2 && foodType == 2 vomits and returns. Pass 0 for neutral when you don't want those effects.

Known break: BuildingEntity.health became a property

On the demo and Playtest builds, BuildingEntity.health is a public field. On the full game it is a public property backed by _health, and its setter also runs CheckDamage(). Any mod compiled against the field throws MissingFieldException: Field not found: single .BuildingEntity.health the moment the full game JITs a method that touches it — including a Harmony prefix or transpiler inlined into BuildingEntity.Update's generated method, which is exactly where it tends to surface.

Route all health access through CUCoreLib's build-tolerant accessor instead of touching the member directly:

using CUCoreLib.Helpers;

// Before (breaks on the full game):
// building.health -= damage;
// if (building.health < 0.5f) return;

// After (works on demo, Playtest, and full):
building.SetHealth(building.GetHealth() - damage);
if (building.GetHealth() < 0.5f) return;

BuildingEntityHealth resolves whichever member the loaded game actually has — property first, field as fallback — once in its static constructor, then caches compiled expression delegates. GetHealth() returns 0f for a null building and SetHealth() no-ops, so the guards stay simple.

Be aware of the behavior change on the full game: because the setter calls CheckDamage(), writing health can trigger destruction logic. CheckDamage() early-returns unless _health < 0.5f (guarded by didDestroyRoutine), so writing healthy values is a no-op — but if you drive health below the break threshold, destruction now happens inside the setter rather than only in Update.

What to do: a practical checklist

  • Prefer name-only Harmony targets for methods that might change. [HarmonyPatch(typeof(Body), "Eat")] binds to the single overload at runtime and survives a parameter-list change. Only pin argument types when you specifically need to select one overload among several.
  • Call changed-signature methods through reflection. Resolve with AccessTools.Method, inspect the parameter count, and build the argument array to match. Cache the MethodInfo so you're not reflecting per call.
  • Use build-tolerant accessors for members that might change shape. A field that becomes a property needs an expression-compiled or reflection-backed accessor, not a direct .health. CUCoreLib's BuildingEntityHealth is the worked example; copy that pattern for other at-risk members.
  • Gate full-game-only patch families with [AppliesToBuild] so they're skipped on the demo before their targets resolve.
  • Watch for MissingFieldException inside a DMD<...> method. A stack frame like BuildingEntity.DMD<BuildingEntity::Update> means a field your patch touched became a property.
  • Test on every build you claim to support. The Playtest build is not the full game — it still has the old field-based shapes, so passing on Playtest does not prove you survive the full game. A build compiling is not the same as a build running; load it in-game on both.
  • Recompile against the full-game Assembly-CSharp once it's available and re-run your patch families. Signature-only diffs miss member-shape changes, so grep your source for direct field access on vanilla types, not just for renamed methods.

What this means for shipping

None of this requires two DLLs. The name-only Harmony target, the reflection invoke helper, and the expression-compiled health accessor all resolve at runtime against whatever build is loaded, so a single demo-compiled DLL keeps working on the full game. The work is up front: find the places you touch vanilla members directly and route them through a tolerant path before the full game reshapes them.

If you hit a break this page doesn't cover, the pattern is the same — identify whether it's a signature change or a member-shape change, then apply the matching tolerant-access technique. Reports of new full-game breaks are welcome in the Discord so they can be documented here and, where it makes sense, absorbed into CUCoreLib itself.
